named_confounds: genre composition shift (juvenile share grows late)
sparse early sample (752 early vs 6014 late works)
rationale: Data: 6766 works, each with one passage (n_passages=1). There are no missing years and no duplicate work IDs. The rate is count__domains__DISTANCE_TRAVEL / n_passages, and works are split at 1876 (late = year >= 1876). Estimand: within each genre I took the mean work rate for late minus early, then averaged across the 8 genres with equal weight. Result: -0.050, with a 95% stratified bootstrap CI of [-0.080, -0.022] from 2000 resamples within genre x period cells. All 8 genres show a decrease, ranging from -0.04 to -0.06. Composition and dating checks: genre mix changes over time (juvenile is a bigger share of late works), but equal-genre weighting neutralises that, and dropping juvenile still gives -0.050. Origin shares are similar across periods. Mean n_editions (1.09 vs 1.08) and author productivity (21.8 vs 20.9 works per author) barely differ. Late works have slightly more high-confidence dates. Robustness: high-confidence dates only gives -0.059 [-0.108, -0.016]; medium gives -0.060; low gives -0.024. By origin: UK -0.043, US -0.087, unknown -0.045. A 1856-1895 window gives -0.051. A WLS adjusting for genre, origin, log editions, date_confidence and log author productivity, with SEs clustered by author, gives -0.052 [-0.078, -0.025]. Caveats: the early period is small (752 works) and the decade-level trend is noisy rather than a sharp step; the early decades of the 1800s are thinly populated. Annotation drift and label noise could matter, since domain tags come from a classifier and confidence varies. The cited passage IDs are only examples of passages tagged DISTANCE_TRAVEL; they do not establish the trend.
